title: Spinoza
summary: Spinoza was a Dutch philosopher who saw the world as one single Nature (which he also called God), where everything follows necessary laws. His Ethics is a path to freedom and quiet joy through understanding yourself and the causes of your feelings.
onEmotions: Spinoza called feelings “affects” and studied them the way a geometer studies lines — without judgment. Every being strives to preserve and strengthen its existence; he called this striving by the Latin word conatus. Joy is a passage to a greater power of living and acting, sadness to a lesser one; all the other feelings are built from these two and from desire. When we don’t understand where a feeling came from, we “undergo” it, as a passion; when we grasp its causes clearly (an “adequate idea”), we become more active and more free.

anxiety.text: Anxiety makes sense: your imagination sketches a future whose outcome is unclear, and the mind is thrown back and forth. Spinoza called this state “vacillation of mind” — being pulled at once by opposite affects, such as hope and fear. For Spinoza, an affect holds us most tightly when its causes are vague to us: we experience it as something that has simply crashed down on us. But once you begin to understand what it is made of — which images, memories and circumstances feed it — you become less of a victim and more of a participant. This doesn’t mean “stop being anxious by willpower.” It means looking at your anxiety with a researcher’s curiosity: it has causes, and simply bringing them into the light already gives you a little room and air.
anxiety.practice: Write down three or four specific thoughts or circumstances that your anxiety is made of right now. Just name them, without trying to solve them.

quote.text: An affect which is a passion ceases to be a passion as soon as we form a clear and distinct idea of it.
quote.author: Baruch Spinoza

fear.text: Fear is natural: every living being strives to preserve itself, and fear is one of the ways that striving shows up. Spinoza defined fear as an inconstant sadness arising from the image of a future or past thing whose outcome we doubt. The key word is “doubt”: fear lives in the uncertainty of the imagination. Spinoza believed that a life led by fear makes us weaker, while a life led by understanding makes us stronger and calmer. He wrote that a free person thinks of nothing less than of death, and that their wisdom is a meditation on life. This isn’t a call to forbid yourself to be afraid. Rather, it’s an invitation to gently shift your gaze from what you fear to what you love and want to keep safe; that is your conatus, your power to live.
fear.practice: Ask yourself: what exactly do I want to protect when I’m afraid? Name it — and notice that behind your fear stands your love for something.

sadness.text: Sadness is a legitimate part of life, and the last thing Spinoza would want is for you to be ashamed of it. For him, sadness is a passage to a lesser power of acting — as if your life energy had been turned down for a while. He studied the affects without moral condemnation, the way one studies the weather or geometric figures. His approach is comforting: sadness doesn’t prove that something is wrong with you; it always has causes, outer and inner. And the more clearly we see those causes, the less sadness rules over us as a blind force. Spinoza also believed that joy, even a small one, restores strength. You don’t have to fight your sadness; you can understand it — and at the same time allow yourself tiny sources of joy beside it.
sadness.practice: Notice when exactly today your sadness grew stronger, and when it eased a little. What was around you in those moments?

grief.text: Grief is a deep sadness over what has been lost, and its weight speaks of the strength of your love. Spinoza was sparing with words of consolation, but one of his observations has helped many people. He noticed that sadness over a lost good softens when a person begins to understand that this good could not have been kept in any way — that the loss is woven into the whole order of nature, rather than having happened through someone’s fault or oversight. This doesn’t cancel the pain, but it lifts from it the tormenting “what if.” Spinoza also taught us to look at things “under the aspect of eternity”: what was, truly was, and nothing can ever undo it. Your love for the one who is gone remains part of you and goes on shaping who you are becoming.
grief.practice: If a “what if…” is tormenting you, try writing that thought down and, next to it, everything you didn’t know back then or that wasn’t up to you.

loneliness.text: Loneliness hurts because people truly need one another — and Spinoza saw this not as a weakness but as a fact of nature. He wrote that nothing is more useful to a human being than another human being who lives by reason: together, people are stronger, and their abilities add up. He also described the “imitation of the affects”: we involuntarily share the feelings of those we see as like ourselves — we rejoice in their joy and grieve in their sadness. So loneliness is a lack of an important source of strength, not a personal failure. At the same time, Spinoza invites you to remember that you are part of one Nature, tied to the world by countless threads even when no one is nearby. Connection starts small: with one shared feeling.
loneliness.practice: Remember someone whose joy once spread to you without your even trying. Could you send them, or someone else, one small message today?

quote.text: To man, then, there is nothing more useful than man.
quote.author: Baruch Spinoza
quote.source: Ethics, Part IV, Scholium to Proposition 18

anger.text: Anger is a strong affect, and most often it arises when we have been harmed or treated unjustly. Spinoza defined anger as the desire to do harm to someone we hate, and he honestly laid out its mechanics: hatred feeds on hatred returned, and grows. But he also noticed that it can be overcome — by love and by what he called “nobility”: a striving, grounded in reason, to help others and join them to ourselves in friendship. This isn’t a demand to suppress your anger and forgive at once. It’s an invitation to understand its causes — including the causes of the other person’s action, who was also moved by their own passions. Understanding weakens anger’s hold and gives you back your freedom to choose.
anger.practice: Try describing the situation that angers you as a researcher would: what causes and passions might have been driving the other person? This isn’t an excuse — just a view from the side.

quote.text: Hate is increased by reciprocal hate, and can, on the other hand, be destroyed by love.
quote.author: Baruch Spinoza

shame.text: Shame is a painful feeling, and everyone who cares about how they live feels it. Spinoza defined shame as sadness accompanied by the idea of some action of ours that we imagine others condemn. He didn’t consider shame a virtue, but he granted it something good: shame shows that the desire to live honorably is alive in a person. Yet the heart of Spinoza’s approach is his gaze without condemnation. He tried not to mock people, not to lament them and not to curse them, but to understand. You can turn that same gaze on yourself: your action had causes, and so do your feelings. Understanding doesn’t cancel responsibility, but it lets you look at yourself not as a defendant, but as a living being who is learning.
shame.practice: Describe what you’re ashamed of in the third person, in a calm tone, as a scientist would: “they did this because…”. What changes?

quote.text: I have taken great care not to laugh at human actions, not to mourn them, and not to curse them, but to understand them.
quote.author: Baruch Spinoza

guilt.text: Guilt tells you that acting well matters to you. Spinoza called a close affect “repentance” — sadness accompanied by the idea of some deed we believe we did from a free decision of the mind. His view here is unusual: Spinoza held that a person’s actions follow from a chain of causes, and the illusion of an “absolutely free decision” only deepens the torment. He even remarked that the one who repents is wretched twice over: first because of the deed, and then because of the sadness about it. This doesn’t mean you can stop thinking about what you did. Rather, it means that understanding is more useful than punishing yourself: sort out the causes, and then turn your strength toward acting differently. Understanding makes a person stronger; self-flagellation makes them weaker.
guilt.practice: Write down what circumstances, feelings and not-knowing led you to that action back then. And then — what you want to do now, building on that understanding.

envy.text: Envy is a very human feeling, and Spinoza explains it without reproach. For him, envy is a kind of hatred in which another’s happiness saddens us and another’s misfortune pleases us. It is born of comparison: the imagination places us next to someone else, and their good seems like our loss. Spinoza offered a remarkable thought: the highest good — understanding, the joy of knowing the world — can belong to everyone at once and doesn’t shrink by being shared. Where the good is common, there is no room for envy. This doesn’t mean outward goods don’t matter. But you can understand envy as a signal of your own desire — and remember that there are goods no one can take from you by gaining them for themselves.
envy.practice: Ask yourself: what do I actually want when I envy? Is there something in this desire that isn’t taken from anyone else if I have it too?

emptiness.text: Emptiness and apathy are a heavy state, and it isn’t your fault. Spinoza’s central idea is conatus: the striving of every thing to persevere in its being. He believed this striving is the very essence of a thing. From this angle, you could say: even when you feel nothing and want nothing, the conatus in you hasn’t disappeared — it is just very quiet, like a fire under ash. The fact that you’re reading these lines, looking for understanding, is already a sign of it. Spinoza believed that the power to live grows from joy, even the smallest, and from understanding. So there’s no need to wait for a great surge of inspiration: it’s enough to notice one tiny “a little better” and let it be.
emptiness.practice: Find one very small thing that makes you even half a degree warmer: tea, light, a sound. Give it one minute.

quote.text: Each thing, as far as it can by its own power, strives to persevere in its being.
quote.author: Baruch Spinoza

confusion.text: Confusion is a natural state when your picture of the world has broken into fragments. Spinoza distinguished “adequate” ideas — clear ones, in which we see the causes — from “inadequate” ones, that is, muddled and fragmentary ideas we pick up through chance experience and other people’s opinions. He didn’t consider muddle a disgrace: at first, most of anyone’s ideas are exactly like that. The path to clarity, for Spinoza, is a gradual clearing-up of connections: what follows from what, what depends on what. He built the Ethics itself step by step, from the simple to the complex. Your confusion is the moment you noticed that the old fragments don’t fit together. And that is already the beginning of understanding, not its absence.
confusion.practice: Choose one part of the situation you feel at least a little sure about, and write it down. Then ask: what follows from this?

fatigue.text: Tiredness is an honest signal from the body, and Spinoza treated the body with respect: for him, mind and body are two sides of one being. When the body is drained, the mind’s power to act weakens too. Spinoza was no stern ascetic. He wrote that it befits a wise person to refresh and restore themselves with moderate, pleasant food and drink, with scents, with the beauty of green plants, with music, games and theater — with everything that can be enjoyed without harm to others. He believed that only grim superstition forbids a person to rejoice. From this angle, rest and pleasure are not a weakness or a reward “for merit,” but a condition for your power to live to recover.
fatigue.practice: Pick one simple thing from Spinoza’s list — music, plants, a good cup of tea, a game — and allow it to yourself today, without feeling you have to earn it.

boredom.text: Everyone knows boredom, and it doesn’t make you any worse. Spinoza has no separate teaching on boredom, but his ideas let us say something important about it. He observed that the human body is made of many parts and needs varied nourishment and experience for all its abilities to stay alive. He also saw that affects often get stuck on a single object and narrow our world. In this light, boredom can be understood as a signal: your power to act has been left idle; it lacks variety and connection with what feeds it. This isn’t a reason to reproach yourself, but an invitation to check which side of your nature hasn’t been given room for a long time.
boredom.practice: Ask yourself: which of my abilities — body, hands, curiosity, company — hasn’t been fed in a long while? What small thing could I give it now?

joy.text: Joy is what Spinoza wished for people more than anything. He defined it as a passage to greater perfection, that is, to a greater power of living and acting. Joy literally makes you more alive. Spinoza distinguished joy that takes hold of just one part of us from “cheerfulness” — joy that fills the whole being; of the latter he wrote that it cannot be excessive and is always good. He also said that laughter and jest are pure good, as long as they don’t mock others. So there’s no need to eye your joy with suspicion or wait for the moment you’ll “have to pay for it.” Let it be: for Spinoza, this is your nature acting freely.
joy.practice: Notice how joy changes your body: your breathing, your shoulders, your face. Stay with that sensation for a few breaths.

love.text: Love and tenderness are warm and very important feelings. Spinoza gave love a simple and deep definition: it is joy accompanied by the idea of an external cause. In other words, we love what increases our power to live, and we connect that joy with a particular person or thing. That is why, he explains, the one who loves naturally strives to have the beloved near and to keep it safe. Tenderness, from this angle, is care for what makes the world more alive for us. Spinoza especially valued love grounded in understanding rather than imagination alone: it is steadier, because it sees the other as they really are. Your tenderness is a sign that the power of joy is at work in you.
love.practice: Think of someone you love. Which particular trait of theirs makes you “more alive”? Name it to yourself.

gratitude.text: Gratitude is one of the brightest feelings. Spinoza defined it as a desire, born of love, to do good to the one who has done good to us. For him it is a natural continuation of joy: we love the cause of our joy and want to answer it in kind. Spinoza wrote that only free people — those guided by reason rather than calculation or fear — are truly grateful to one another. Their gratitude isn’t like an exchange of favors: it is friendship. From this angle, your gratitude isn’t a debt to be repaid, but a bond that strengthens you both. You can simply feel it and, if you like, express it.
gratitude.practice: Name one person you’re grateful to right now and one specific thing they did. Do you feel like telling them somehow?

hope.text: Hope is an understandable and life-giving feeling. Spinoza defined it as an inconstant joy arising from the image of a future thing whose outcome we doubt. He was honest: since the outcome is doubtful, hope always lives next door to fear. That’s why he wrote that hope in itself is not yet the highest good — it tells us how much we don’t know. But this isn’t a call to give up hope. For Spinoza, as uncertainty shrinks and we better understand what we can do, hope can grow into “confidence” — a calm joy that doesn’t depend on swings. You can cherish your hope and, little by little, turn it into understanding: what here is within my power?
hope.practice: Write down what you hope for and, next to it, one thing you already know or can do in that direction.

quote.text: There is neither hope without fear, nor fear without hope.
quote.author: Baruch Spinoza
quote.source: Ethics, Part III, Definitions of the Affects, Explanation of 13

nostalgia.text: Nostalgia is a subtle feeling in which love and sadness meet. Spinoza has a strikingly precise definition for it: “longing” (desiderium) is a desire to possess a thing, kept alive by the memory of it and at the same time held back by the memory of other things that exclude its existence. Put simply: memory calls us back there, and the knowledge that that time is gone holds us back. Hence both the sweetness and the bitterness. Spinoza helps us see that nostalgia isn’t a weakness but the work of memory and love. It shows that you were once happy, and that you have the capacity for that kind of joy. You don’t need to bring the past back to find in it a clue about what is dear to you.
nostalgia.practice: Remember what you miss and ask yourself: what feeling was at the heart of that time — lightness, closeness, freedom? Where could it find a place now?

craving.text: A craving is a sharp “I want it right now,” and it can be very strong. Spinoza looked at desire without condemnation: he called it the very essence of a human being, an expression of conatus — the striving to live and preserve oneself. The trouble isn’t the desire itself, but the way imagination ties it to a single object and paints that object as the only path to relief. Spinoza noted that an affect toward a thing we imagine as near and available “now” is stronger than one toward a future thing, even a far more important one. And he warned soberly: an affect can’t simply be forbidden — it can only be weakened by another, stronger affect. So it helps not to argue with the craving, but to look beside it for something living that gives you strength, however small.
craving.practice: Ask yourself: “What relief am I expecting from this right now?” Name that relief — calm, warmth, rest — and think about what else could give you even a little of it.

quote.text: An affect cannot be restrained or taken away except by an affect opposite to, and stronger than, the affect to be restrained.
quote.author: Baruch Spinoza

addiction.text: Addiction is not a moral failure. Spinoza would have called it one form of what he named “bondage”: a state in which we are governed by external causes and passions rather than by our own understanding. Importantly, for Spinoza bondage is the common lot of humankind, not the fault of one individual; he studied it as a natural phenomenon, without mockery or curses. At the opening of his unfinished Treatise on the Emendation of the Intellect, he honestly admits that he himself had seen how the pursuit of wealth, honor and sensual pleasure can take over the mind so completely that it can hardly think of anything else. The path to freedom, for Spinoza, runs not through self-flagellation but through gradually understanding your affects and seeking joys that strengthen rather than empty you.
addiction.practice: Write down what the thing your addiction is organized around meant to you at the very beginning: what did it give you? This isn’t an excuse, but a first step toward understanding. If you feel like it, you can talk about this with someone who knows this path from the inside.

quote.text: Man’s lack of power to moderate and restrain the affects I call bondage.
quote.author: Baruch Spinoza

hangover.text: A hangover morning is hard on both body and soul: anxiety, shame, gaps in memory. Spinoza would say there is nothing mysterious here. For him the mind is “the idea of the body”: when the body’s power decreases, so does the mind’s, so this morning’s dark thoughts are largely dictated by an exhausted body. Spinoza even has an observation that fits almost word for word: the drunk, he wrote, believes he speaks from a free decision of the mind things that, once sober, he would rather have kept to himself. He gave this example not as a reproach, but to show how little free we are when external causes move us. Understanding this lifts some needless weight from the soul: yesterday’s “you” acted under a strong influence, and today’s “you” can calmly sort things out once you’ve recovered.
hangover.practice: Today, just one thing: water, food, rest. If conversations about yesterday are needed, put them off until you feel stronger.

euphoria.text: A burst of euphoria is a strong joy, and Spinoza is not at all against joy: for him it is a passage to a greater power of living. But he distinguished two kinds of it. “Cheerfulness” takes hold of the whole body and the whole mind at once and, for Spinoza, cannot be excessive. What he called “titillation” — an excited joy that affects one part of us more than the rest — can flare up so strongly that it blocks out everything else. This isn’t a reason to spoil your celebration. Rather, it’s a way to live it more attentively: to notice whether the high fills you wholly — body, thoughts, relationships — or seizes just one side. That attention in itself, for Spinoza, makes joy more your own, more active — and therefore more lasting.
euphoria.practice: Look inside yourself: where is this joy felt — in your body, in your thoughts, in the wish to share it with someone? Just notice.

crash.text: A sharp drop after a high is a painful state, and it isn’t your fault. Spinoza has an idea that helps here unexpectedly. He defined joy and sadness not as states but as passages: joy is a passage to a greater power of acting, sadness to a lesser. From this angle, the crash is a movement, not a new truth about you and your life. It feels especially sharp because imagination compares “now” with the peak you’ve just lived through. Spinoza advised looking into the causes of an affect: what exactly lifted you, and what has changed. As the causes become clearer, the crash stops feeling like the world collapsing and becomes an understandable ebb after the tide.
crash.practice: Finish the sentence: “Things feel harder right now because…” — and name one specific cause, not a verdict on yourself.

panic.text: A panic attack is one of the most frightening experiences: a wave of terror sweeps over you, and your body seems to slip out of control. Spinoza described a related affect, “consternation”: a state in which the desire to avoid harm is paralyzed by astonishment at what we fear. It’s an honest admission: fear can be so strong that it keeps us from even moving. But Spinoza also offers something to lean on: mind and body are two sides of one being, and everything that happens in the body is reflected in the mind. So what helps isn’t arguing with the terror, but returning to the body — to what it feels right now. A wave like this usually rises, peaks and subsides within a few minutes. You don’t need to decide anything — just breathe and wait.
panic.practice: Press your feet into the floor, put a hand on your chest or belly, and take a few breaths with a long, slow exhale. Name out loud three things you can see.

dread.text: Existential dread — “what’s the point of it all,” the feeling of an abyss — comes to thoughtful people, and there’s no need to be ashamed of it. Spinoza answered it with his whole philosophy. For him a human being is part of infinite Nature, one of its living expressions, and the essence of each of us is conatus, the striving to live. He wrote that a free person thinks of nothing less than of death, and that their wisdom is a meditation on life. This isn’t a call to close your eyes. It’s an invitation to change where you’re looking from: the abyss looks like an abyss when we see ourselves as separate and alone. But when we understand ourselves as part of a large, living whole, the question “what for?” gets a simple answer: to live, to act and to rejoice — as far as it is in our power.
dread.practice: Name one thing that adds to your power to live today — a person, a sound, an activity. Stay with it in your mind for a minute.

quote.text: A free man thinks of nothing less than of death, and his wisdom is a meditation on life, not on death.
quote.author: Baruch Spinoza

fomo.text: The fear of missing out is a very human feeling: it seems that everyone else is living more vividly, and you’re not where it’s happening. Spinoza described its roots as early as the Treatise on the Emendation of the Intellect. He noticed that chasing honor and recognition forces us to live with an eye on people’s opinions: to seek what they seek and avoid what they avoid. Later, in the Ethics, he called the immoderate desire for glory “ambition” and showed how it feeds on the imitation of others’ affects: we want what we imagine others want. From this angle, the fear of missing out isn’t your personal flaw but a mechanism of the imagination. You can notice it and ask: do I want this myself, or do I just see that others want it?
fomo.practice: Pick one “I should be there” and ask: if no one ever found out about it, would I want it? Write down the honest answer.

sleepless.text: Lying awake with thoughts at three in the morning is exhausting, and very many people know it. Spinoza would explain why thoughts seem so real at night. He wrote that the mind imagines a thing as present until the body receives an impression that excludes its existence. During the day there are plenty of such “excluding” impressions: people, tasks, light. At night there are almost none, and imagined troubles freely take up all the space, as if they were happening right now. This doesn’t mean you see the truth more clearly — on the contrary, you see it less well. Understanding this mechanism can loosen the grip of night thoughts a little: they are loud, but no more reliable than they are by day.
sleepless.practice: Give your body one real, “excluding” impression: feel the fabric of the blanket, the coolness of the pillow, the weight of your hands. Stay with that sensation.

betrayal.text: Betrayal wounds deeply because the blow comes from someone we loved or trusted. Spinoza described exactly why it hurts so much. He wrote that if we begin to hate what we once loved, that hatred can be greater than if we had never loved at all — because sadness over the lost love is added to it. So the strength of your pain is a measure of how open you were. Spinoza did not demand immediate forgiveness. He suggested gradually coming to understand — both your own feelings and the causes that moved the other person. Understanding doesn’t justify the betrayal, but it slowly gives you back the strength that powerless hatred takes away.
betrayal.practice: Write down what exactly in this story was valuable to you — trust, closeness, a shared purpose. That is what you still have, even if the person is gone.

jealousy.text: Jealousy is agonizing, and Spinoza described it with rare precision. He defined it as a vacillation of mind in which love and hatred for the beloved live side by side, mixed with envy toward a rival. Jealousy is especially hard, he observed, because the imagination paints painful pictures of its own accord and returns to them again and again. Spinoza didn’t shame this feeling — he saw it as a natural consequence of a love that depends on what doesn’t belong to us. His path is understanding: telling apart what you actually know from what imagination fills in. This doesn’t make your love smaller, but it reduces the power of pictures that torment you more than the facts do.
jealousy.practice: When a painful picture comes, name it: “this is an image, not a fact.” Then shift your gaze to something real in front of you.

resentment.text: An old grudge is a weight you carry against your will. Spinoza would take it seriously: you were hurt, and sadness accompanied by the idea of its cause is exactly what he defined as hatred. But he also has practical advice that sounds strikingly modern. He suggested not clinging to the image of the offense, but understanding that people’s actions follow from a chain of causes — and preparing yourself for wrongs in advance, taking care to answer them not with hatred but with nobility. Spinoza noted that a mind that understands things as necessary suffers less from them. Letting go of a grudge here means not forgiving out of duty, but ceasing to hand over your power to live to it. This happens gradually, and there’s no need to hurry.
resentment.practice: Describe the grudge in one sentence the way a calm historian would: what happened and what causes might have been behind it.

heartbreak.text: A broken heart hurts, and the pain shows how much this person meant to you. Spinoza defined love as joy connected with the idea of its external cause. When the cause goes away, the joy doesn’t vanish without a trace at once: memory calls us again and again to where things were good. Spinoza saw deeper still: people suffer most from loving what is changeable and never fully in our power. This isn’t a reproach for having loved — that is how all people love. But it is a hint: alongside a love that wounds, you can grow joys no one can take away — understanding, friendship, your own pursuits. They won’t replace what was lost, but they will give your heart something to rest on.
heartbreak.practice: Name one joy that belongs to you alone and doesn’t depend on the relationship that ended. Give it a little time today.

impostor.text: The fear of being found out — “I’m not who they take me for” — is felt by very many people, clever and experienced ones included. Spinoza has a precise word for one part of it: “self-abasement” — when, under the influence of sadness, a person thinks less of themselves than is fair. Spinoza considered it just as much a distortion as pride, only pointing the other way: both arise from unclear, incomplete ideas about oneself. Its opposite is “self-esteem,” a joy born when a person clearly sees their real power of acting. This isn’t overconfidence but sobriety. Try looking at yourself as a researcher, not as a defendant: what can you actually do, and what do you actually do?
impostor.practice: Write down three specific things you’ve done well — not impressions of yourself, but facts.

self_hatred.text: Self-hatred is a very heavy feeling, and the inner critic can speak loudly and convincingly. But Spinoza would not agree with it. For him the essence of every person is conatus, the striving to live, and by its very nature it aims at preserving and strengthening oneself, not at destruction. If a voice inside you hates you, then for Spinoza it is the result of external causes: other people’s words, hurts you’ve lived through, images absorbed long ago. Such a voice doesn’t reveal the truth about you; it shows what has happened to you. Spinoza believed that self-esteem grounded in understanding is perhaps the highest thing we can hope for. The way to it isn’t punishment, but understanding yourself without mockery or curses.
self_hatred.practice: Ask your inner critic: “Whose voice are you speaking in?” Write down whose it reminds you of — this helps separate it from you.

helplessness.text: Helplessness is a heavy experience, and Spinoza knew perfectly well that human beings are not all-powerful. At the end of the fourth part of the Ethics he writes plainly: our power is limited and is infinitely surpassed by the power of external causes, so we cannot adapt everything outside us to our use. But he adds a consolation that helps many people: if we understand that we did what was in our power, and that our power could not reach further, then the better part of us can calmly accept what happens. This isn’t passivity. It’s an honest distinction: here is where my possibilities end — and here is what, within that boundary, I still can do. Helplessness before something large doesn’t cancel your strength in something small.
helplessness.practice: Finish the sentence: “This is not in my power, and it is not my fault. But here is what I can do today: …” — one small action.

procrastination.text: “I can’t get started” is a state that’s easy to mistake for laziness, though it isn’t laziness. Spinoza described its mechanism precisely. He quoted Ovid’s line — “I see the better and approve it, but I follow the worse” — and explained why this happens. True knowledge of what is good, he wrote, cannot by itself restrain an affect — only insofar as it becomes an affect itself, that is, takes on the color of feeling. That’s why pep talks of the “I must, I must” kind usually don’t work: they remain knowledge without force. What works is something else — finding even a drop of joy, interest or relief in the task. Spinoza helps you stop shaming yourself and look not for more discipline, but for more living feeling connected with the beginning.
procrastination.practice: Ask yourself: “What in this task could be even a tiny bit interesting or pleasant for me?” Start with exactly that part.

uprooted.text: Being cut off from home is a deep loss, and Spinoza knew it firsthand. At twenty-three he was expelled from the Jewish community of Amsterdam in which he had grown up; later he left the city and lived in small Dutch towns, earning his living by grinding lenses. He lost his former circle, but he built a new one — of friends and interlocutors with whom he corresponded and argued. In his philosophy a human being is part of one Nature, and that belonging doesn’t depend on a city or a country: wherever you are, you remain part of the whole. But Spinoza also held that nothing is more useful to a person than another person. From this angle, roots in a new place grow not through the landscape but through connections.
uprooted.practice: Name one person in your new place you’d like to talk with a little more. Think about what small step toward that is possible this week.

overload.text: Overload from an endless stream of information is a real burden on the mind, not your weakness. Surprisingly, Spinoza explained what happens to us in such moments. He wrote that the human body can distinctly perceive only a limited number of images at once. When there are more, they begin to blur together, and the mind stops telling one thing from another — everything merges into a general, vague “something.” For Spinoza this was a property of the body’s nature, not a flaw of character. Hence a simple conclusion: clarity returns when there are fewer images. You don’t need to keep up with everything — you need to give your mind a chance to see one thing distinctly again.
overload.practice: Put the screen aside for five minutes and look closely at one object nearby: its shape, color, texture. Let your mind see one thing whole.

unreality.text: The sense of unreality — when the world or you yourself seem not quite real — is frightening, and it deserves to be described with care. Here Spinoza offers something to lean on in his central idea about human beings: the mind is “the idea of the body.” We know ourselves and the world first of all through how the body feels and responds. When the link with bodily sensations seems to weaken, the world can seem flat and distant, like a picture. From this angle, you could say the way back leads not through thinking about whether everything is real, but through simple sensations: warmth, weight, touch, breath. The body is your most direct connection with reality, and in it you always have a point of presence.
unreality.practice: Touch something with a distinct texture — wood, fabric, cool glass. Describe to yourself three sensations you feel.

awe.text: Awe before something vast or beautiful is a rare experience, and worth treasuring. Spinoza described “wonder” as a state in which the mind lingers on something singular, because that image resembles nothing familiar and isn’t connected with others. And love for what we wonder at he called “devotion.” But Spinoza also offers a deeper dimension of awe: what he called “the intellectual love of God” — the joy of understanding how everything in Nature is connected. For him, awe before the world doesn’t contradict reason; it can become its summit. From this angle, your awe is a moment when you felt yourself part of something immense. Let it last.
awe.practice: Try to notice what the thing that stirred your awe is connected with: where it came from, what it is a part of. Stay in that sense of connection.

relief.text: Relief is a bright feeling, and Spinoza has an almost exact name for it. He defined “gladness” as joy accompanied by the idea of a past thing that turned out better than we had hoped. There is an important detail in this definition: relief always carries the memory of fear. That’s exactly why it is felt so strongly — the joy here is measured by how tense the waiting was. For Spinoza every joy is a passage to a greater power of living, so relief literally gives you back your strength. There’s no need to rush on or to devalue it with “it could have been worse.” Allow yourself this passage — body and mind recover precisely in moments like these.
relief.practice: Notice what strength has come back to you along with the relief: what do you feel like doing now, what do you have more energy for?

calm.text: Calm is a precious state, and for Spinoza it was the goal of the whole Ethics. He called it “true peace of mind” and said that the wise person, who understands themselves and the world as part of the necessary order of Nature, is rarely troubled in spirit. An important thought of Spinoza’s: this calm is not a reward to be earned, nor a lull before the storm. It is itself the good — what he called blessedness. Calm here isn’t emptiness or indifference: it is a clarity in which joy becomes quiet and steady. If you feel it now, there’s no need to ask “how long will it last.” You can simply be in it and notice how it is made.
calm.practice: Notice what thoughts, sensations or circumstances accompany your calm. Remember at least one of them.

quote.text: Blessedness is not the reward of virtue, but virtue itself.
quote.author: Baruch Spinoza

inspiration.text: Inspiration is one of the most joyful states, and Spinoza would explain why it feels the way it does. He distinguished affects that we “undergo” from external causes from joy that arises out of our own activity — when we ourselves are the cause of what happens. From this angle, inspiration is a moment when your conatus acts freely and at full strength: you aren’t being pushed; you are creating. Spinoza believed that human abilities are wider than we usually think, and that no one has yet determined what the body can do. Allow yourself this lift. It shows you what strength is in you — and that it can appear again.
inspiration.practice: Write down what exactly inspires you now, and where you feel yourself to be the cause rather than a spectator. Mark the first small step.

quote.text: No one has yet determined what the body can do.
quote.author: Baruch Spinoza
quote.source: Ethics, Part III, Scholium to Proposition 2

schadenfreude.text: Schadenfreude is a feeling almost no one admits to, but almost everyone knows. Spinoza described it without a shadow of reproach. In the Ethics he shows the mechanics: if we hate or envy someone, then when we imagine their misfortune, we feel joy. That is exactly how he defined envy — as sadness at another’s happiness and joy at another’s misfortune. So schadenfreude isn’t a sign that you’re rotten, but the trace of another, earlier affect: a hurt, envy, a sense of injustice. Spinoza would add: such joy is fragile, because it depends on other people’s falls rather than on your own strength. It helps neither to chase it away nor to be ashamed of it, but to ask: what pain in me has just found relief?
schadenfreude.practice: Write down who this person is to you and what happened between you before. What old feeling — a hurt, envy, weariness from comparison — stands behind today’s joy?

contempt.text: Contempt can be cold and even pleasant: it seems to set us above the other. Spinoza distinguished two affects here. “Disregard” — when a thing touches the mind so little that we notice in it what isn’t there rather than what is. And “scorn” (despectus) he defined as thinking less of someone than is fair, out of hatred. Notice the words “less than is fair”: for Spinoza, contempt is a distortion of the picture, not a sober assessment. It usually grows out of being hurt: the person caused us sadness, and the imagination shrinks them. This isn’t a reason to reproach yourself. But you can check: what do I know about the causes that made this person the way they are? Understanding causes, Spinoza said, gradually frees us from the need to look down on others — and from the weariness that comes with it.
contempt.practice: Write three facts about the person you feel contempt for, without judgment — just what they do and in what circumstances. Notice whether anything in the feeling shifts.

disgust.text: Disgust is an ancient, bodily feeling: you want to pull away, shut yourself off, not see. Spinoza explained it very soberly. He wrote that any thing can “by accident” become a cause of sadness or joy for us — simply because it once happened to be near something that affected us. Hence his definition: “aversion” (aversio) is sadness accompanied by the idea of a thing that has accidentally become its cause. In other words, disgust often says more about our history than about the object itself. This applies to disgust with yourself too: it may also be a trace of old associations and other people’s words, not the truth about you. Spinoza didn’t demand that we force ourselves to love what repels us. He suggested understanding which associations the feeling is made of — and then it stops being a verdict.
disgust.practice: Ask yourself: what else in my life is this image or person connected with? Write down the first association that comes, without judging it.

revenge.text: The wish for revenge is a natural response to pain inflicted on you, and Spinoza didn’t pretend it doesn’t exist. He defined “vengeance” as the desire by which, from reciprocal hatred, we are moved to do harm to someone who has harmed us. And right away he showed the trap: hatred answered with hatred only grows. Revenge ties us to the one who hurt us: we go on living their deed, thinking about them, depending on them. Spinoza proposed another path — not as a moral demand, but as a path to your own strength: to answer hostility with “nobility,” that is, with an action of reason that strengthens us ourselves. This doesn’t mean the hurt doesn’t matter. It means you can hear out the wish for revenge as a cry for justice — and look for a form for it that won’t take away your freedom.
revenge.practice: Write down: what does my wish for revenge really want — acknowledgment, justice, safety? What small step toward that is possible without harming anyone?

quote.text: He who lives according to the guidance of reason strives, as far as he can, to repay the other’s hate, anger, and disdain, etc., toward him, with love, or nobility.
quote.author: Baruch Spinoza

anger_at_loved.text: Being angry at the people you love is one of the most ordinary experiences — and one of the most shameful-feeling. Spinoza would explain why it is so strong: the more closely a person is bound up with our life, the more strongly they can affect us — with joy and with sadness alike. We expect a lot from those close to us, and every disappointment hits more precisely. Spinoza noticed something else: we get angrier when we believe the other “freely” chose to hurt us, and softer when we see the necessary causes of their actions. Your partner, parent or child is also moved by their nature, their tiredness, their fears — just as you are. Understanding this doesn’t make your anger “wrong.” It helps you not turn it into words and actions you’ll regret later, and to see it as a signal: something here matters to me.
anger_at_loved.practice: When anger at someone close rises again, say to yourself: “there are causes for this — theirs and mine.” Take three slow breaths out before you respond.

ambivalence.text: Loving someone and at the same time not being able to stand them is neither strange nor hypocritical. Spinoza gave an exact description of it. If one and the same thing is connected for us with both joy and sadness, we will love and hate it at once; he called this state “vacillation of mind” (fluctuatio animi) and compared it to doubt: the mind is pulled in two directions at once. Most often this happens precisely with those close to us: we share too many joys and too many wounds with them. Spinoza didn’t demand that we choose one feeling and renounce the other. He suggested distinguishing: which particular traits, actions and memories bring joy, and which bring sadness. When the mixture comes apart into understandable pieces, it stops being an agonizing riddle and becomes a map of your relationship.
ambivalence.practice: Divide a page into two columns: “what in this person gladdens me” and “what wounds me.” Don’t look for a total — just let both columns exist.

guilty_relief.text: Relief after a breakup, after someone leaves, or after a loved one’s long illness often comes together with shame: “how can I feel this?” Spinoza would help you see here not a contradiction, but natural mechanics. Joy, by his definition, is a passage to a greater power of living. When a long stretch of strain, fear or powerlessness ends, the returning strength is inevitably felt as relief. This doesn’t mean you didn’t love: the sadness of loss and the joy of release from a burden can live in you at the same time, because they are tied to different sides of one story. Spinoza tried not to mock or curse human affects, but to understand them. Your relief is a signal of how much strength what you went through was taking, not a verdict on your love.
guilty_relief.practice: Finish two sentences: “It’s easier for me because … has ended” and “It hurts because I loved…”. Let both be true.

indifference.text: Sometimes an event “ought” to move you — someone else’s grief, an important date, someone’s joy — and inside there is silence. That’s frightening: have you gone cold? Spinoza looked at this more calmly. He wrote that different people can be affected differently by one and the same object, and even one person differently at different times. An affect isn’t an obligation or a test of your humanity, but an event that arises from the meeting of your body and mind with the world in a particular state. Tiredness, overload, old pain can muffle the response. From Spinoza’s point of view, you could say that indifference, too, is a state with its own causes, not an empty space. Asking about its causes is more honest than acting out a feeling that isn’t there. Often the response comes later, once the soul has the strength.
indifference.practice: Notice what state you’re in right now: how much you’ve slept, how much has piled up on you lately. Write it down without reproach — like the weather in which the event happened.

escape.text: The wish to drop everything — your job, your city, your familiar role — tells you that somewhere your power to live is being squeezed. Spinoza would call this the work of conatus, the striving to preserve and strengthen one’s being: the mind, he wrote, strives to imagine what increases its power and to push away what diminishes it. So the dream of escape isn’t weakness but an understandable signal. Spinoza did, however, distinguish fleeing from sadness from moving toward joy. The first is governed by an external cause, which can follow us anywhere; the second rests on understanding what actually nourishes us. Interestingly, he didn’t consider leaving cowardly: the virtue of a free person, he said, shows just as much in avoiding dangers as in overcoming them. What matters is understanding what you’re moving away from and what you’re moving toward.
escape.practice: Describe in two or three sentences the place or life you want to escape to. What exactly is there — quiet, freedom, respect? Where could even a drop of it be possible this very week?

forbidden_attraction.text: Attraction to someone who is unavailable or “the wrong person” often brings confusion and guilt. Spinoza suggested looking at desire without the usual moral court. Desire, he wrote, is the very essence of a human being: it is our striving to exist, conscious of itself. And he made a striking observation: we don’t desire something because we judge it good — on the contrary, we judge something good because we desire it. So the attraction itself says nothing yet about what is “right”; it says something about you — about what in you is looking for life. Spinoza would give no order here, either to act or to forbid yourself to feel. He would suggest understanding: what image, what promise of joy does this person hold for you? A desire that is understood stops steering us blindly.
forbidden_attraction.practice: Without naming the person, write down: what quality or feeling in them draws me? Where else in my life could it find a place?

quote.text: We neither strive for, nor will, neither want, nor desire anything because we judge it to be good; on the contrary, we judge something to be good because we strive for it, will it, want it, and desire it.
quote.author: Baruch Spinoza
quote.source: Ethics, Part III, Scholium to Proposition 9

social_anxiety.text: Fear of people and their judgment can grip you so tightly that it’s hard to say a word. Spinoza explained it through a mechanism he called “the imitation of the affects”: we involuntarily take on the feelings of those who are like us, and that’s why we pick up their joy or displeasure so keenly. From this comes the striving to do what we imagine will please people; Spinoza noticed that when it becomes excessive, it turns into dependence on others’ approval. The word “imagine” matters: we react not to what others think, but to what our imagination paints. Spinoza didn’t call on us to stop noticing others — nothing, he believed, is more useful to a person than another person. He suggested shifting your footing: from imagined judgments to clear knowledge of your own actions and of what is dear to you.
social_anxiety.practice: After spending time with people, write down one thing you actually saw or heard, and one thing you only imagined about what others were thinking. Compare them.

uncertainty.text: When it’s unclear what will happen, the mind rushes between options, and that is exhausting. Spinoza knew where this torment comes from: feelings about a future we are unsure of swing between hope and fear. But he also offered an unexpected support. The more we understand things as necessary — as the results of chains of causes rather than whims of chance — the less we suffer from the affects. This isn’t fatalism or “nothing can be done.” It’s a view in which you see that whatever happens will have causes, many of which are already at work, and some of which are you yourself, your actions. Spinoza called the highest form of this view understanding things “under the aspect of eternity” — calm and wide. Uncertainty doesn’t disappear, but it stops looking like chaos.
uncertainty.practice: Draw three columns: what is already known, what depends on me, what doesn’t depend on me right now. Choose one action from the middle column.

quote.text: Insofar as the mind understands all things as necessary, it has a greater power over the affects, or is less acted on by them.
quote.author: Baruch Spinoza

waiting.text: Waiting is a strange state: life seems to be on pause, while your thoughts keep running ahead again and again. Spinoza noticed that images of the future act on us through the imagination: it either inflates them or tosses us between “it’ll work out” and “it won’t.” He believed that reason can relate to the future and the present more evenly, not letting an event that hasn’t yet happened take over your whole life. The key to his approach is that conatus, the striving to exist, doesn’t stop while you wait. You go on living and acting now, and the joy of a small action in which you yourself are the cause is real today — unlike the imagined outcomes. There’s no need to hurry the waiting; you can simply give it back its proper place among other things.
waiting.practice: Choose one small task that depends only on you and can be finished today. Do it, and notice how your own action feels against the background of waiting.

regret.text: Regret over what you did or didn’t do can come back again and again. Spinoza looked at it strictly, but — strange as it may seem — in a freeing way. He wrote that repentance is not a virtue: the one who repents suffers twice — first from the deed, then from the sadness about it. This isn’t a call to indifference. Spinoza valued understanding highly: seeing what causes — not knowing, fear, tiredness, circumstances — led to that choice. Given the causes at work back then, the past could not have been otherwise; but your understanding has changed now, and it is already changing the future. From this angle, regret is useful exactly to the extent that it turns into knowledge rather than endless self-punishment.
regret.practice: Write down: what did I know and feel back then, when I made that decision? And what do I know now that I didn’t know then?

quote.text: Repentance is not a virtue, or does not arise from reason; instead, he who repents what he did is twice miserable, or lacks power.
quote.author: Baruch Spinoza

longing.text: Longing for a particular person is one of the few feelings Spinoza defined directly. He called it desiderium: a desire to possess a thing, kept alive by the memory of it and at the same time held back by the memory of what excludes its presence. The whole mechanics of longing is in this definition: memory brings the person back to you again — their voice, their habits — and immediately runs into the fact that they aren’t here. Spinoza also explained why you want to bring back precisely the circumstances in which you were happy together: imagination links joy with the whole picture at once. Longing, then, is the other side of love, of a joy that is still in you. There’s no need to chase it away; it tells you that this bond is still alive.
longing.practice: Remember one specific moment with this person — the place, the light, the words. Stay with it for a minute, then notice which quality of that moment is especially dear to you.

world_pain.text: Heavy news, war, injustice — pain for the world is natural for anyone who can feel. Spinoza explained it through “the imitation of the affects”: when we imagine the suffering of a being like us, we feel sadness ourselves. He called this feeling “pity,” and his assessment of it was honest to the point of discomfort: sadness in itself, for Spinoza, diminishes our power, and the one who lives by reason strives not so much to suffer along as to actively help. But he also added that someone moved to help others neither by reason nor by pity is rightly called inhuman. Your pain is a sign of your humanity. Spinoza would help you take the next step: to turn it from powerless sadness into action, however small — and to protect your strength, because only someone who has strength can carry something to others.
world_pain.practice: Choose one small, real action for others — to help, support, share — and do it. Then limit your news time for today.

quote.text: He who is moved to aid others neither by reason nor by pity is rightly called inhuman.
quote.author: Baruch Spinoza
quote.source: Ethics, Part IV, Scholium to Proposition 50

rejection.text: Rejection wounds deeply: it seems that it wasn’t an offer, a friendship or a job that was turned down, but you as a whole. Spinoza would help separate these things. After a refusal, sadness easily turns into what he called “self-abasement” (abjectio) — an opinion of yourself, born of sadness, that is lower than is fair. The words “lower than is fair” matter: this is a distortion, not the truth about you. The other person’s decision flows from their nature, history, circumstances and desires — a long chain of causes in which you are only one link. According to Spinoza, we suffer less from what we understand as the result of necessary causes rather than as a verdict. A refusal tells you how two different natures met at a particular moment — but it doesn’t measure your worth.
rejection.practice: Write down three things you can do or have done well, regardless of this person. Read them out loud.

abandonment.text: The fear of being abandoned keeps you on edge: every silence seems like a sign, every delay like a threat. Spinoza saw fear as a sadness that grows from doubt: the future is unclear, and imagination paints the worst outcome. He also noticed that we worry most about what we love when it is changeable and not fully in our power. And people are never fully in our power. Spinoza offered a wise move: an affect connected with many different causes is less burdensome than one chained to a single cause. When all your joy rests on one person, any step they take aside feels like a cliff edge. When it has many supports — friendship, work, the body, understanding — your love for this person remains, but fear loses its absolute power.
abandonment.practice: Draw yourself in the center of a page and connect yourself with lines to everything that gives you joy and support: people, activities, places. Look at how many connections there are.

unrequited.text: Unrequited love hurts in a special way: the feeling is alive, but there is no answer. Spinoza defined love as joy accompanied by the idea of its external cause. Notice: there is no reciprocity in this definition. Love is your joy, and it is real even if the other person doesn’t share it. The pain comes from the fact that, when we love, we naturally strive to be loved in return, and when that striving meets refusal, sadness arises. Spinoza would remind you: the other person follows their own nature, and another’s love can’t be summoned by effort or by merit. That is bitter, but also freeing — you haven’t failed an exam. From his point of view, you could say: your capacity to love like this is a strength that belongs to you, and it doesn’t vanish because it found no answer here.
unrequited.practice: Write down what exactly this love awakened in you — which qualities, desires, strengths. That is yours, and it will stay with you.

humiliation.text: Humiliation burns: it seems you’ve been made smaller — in front of others or in your own eyes. Spinoza would help you see what it is made of. We involuntarily take on other people’s feelings, he wrote. So when we are treated with disdain, we begin to look at ourselves through their eyes and feel toward ourselves what we imagine they feel. Spinoza warned about something else, too: self-respect that rests only on the opinion of the crowd is always fragile — it has to be anxiously defended every day. A steadier support is one grounded in understanding your own actions. From this angle, it’s important to separate the event from the conclusion: you were treated in a humiliating way — that is a fact about the other person’s action. “I am worthless” is someone else’s affect that for a moment you took for your own.
humiliation.practice: Write on one line what exactly happened, and on another what conclusion about yourself this event is pressing on you. Note that the second line is not a fact, but someone else’s view.

body_shame.text: Dissatisfaction with your body can be painful and exhausting, and it is very common. Spinoza offered a view that changes the very framing of the question. For him mind and body are not a master and a faulty tool, but one and the same being seen from two sides: the mind is the idea of the body. From this angle, waging war on your body means partly waging war on yourself. As for beauty and ugliness, Spinoza wrote plainly in the appendix to the first part of the Ethics that people call things beautiful or ugly depending on how they affect their imagination — these are ways of imagining, not properties of the things themselves. The yardsticks used to judge bodies change from era to era. A more reliable question, following Spinoza: what can this body do? What does it let you feel and do?
body_shame.practice: Name three things your body has let you do or feel over the past week. Write them down without any judgments about appearance.

illness.text: When the body lets you down, it isn’t only the body that suffers: your mood, your thoughts, your sense of yourself change too. Spinoza explained this by the unity of mind and body: whatever diminishes the body’s power to act diminishes the mind’s power to think as well. So tiredness, irritability and sadness during illness aren’t a weakness of character but a natural consequence. Spinoza himself apparently suffered from a lung illness for many years and went on working as far as his strength allowed. He didn’t promise that understanding would heal the body. But he showed that even within limits there remains room for activity: understanding what is happening, noticing the small joys that are still within reach, being the cause of at least a few small events in your day. This doesn’t cancel the pain, but it gives you back a little strength.
illness.practice: Today, notice one small action in which you yourself are the cause: you chose what to read, whom to write to, how to sit more comfortably. That, too, is your strength.

pride.text: Pride in something you’ve done is a good feeling, and Spinoza would be glad for you. He distinguished two very different affects. “Pride” in the sense of arrogance — thinking more highly of yourself than is fair, born of self-love and fed by comparison with others. And “self-esteem” (acquiescentia in se ipso) — a joy that arises when a person contemplates themselves and their power of acting. Spinoza valued the second very highly: self-esteem born of reason he called the highest thing we can hope for. The difference is simple: arrogance needs someone below, while self-esteem needs only a clear view of your own action. You did something, and you are its cause. Let yourself see that and be glad: such joy, for Spinoza, doesn’t puff a person up — it makes them stronger and more generous.
pride.practice: Write down what exactly you did and which of your qualities it took. Read it through and give yourself a minute simply to be glad.

melancholy.text: Bright sadness is a subtle feeling in which sorrow mingles with tenderness and memory. Spinoza used the word “melancholy” in a narrower sense: that was his name for a sadness that takes hold of the whole person, and he considered it always harmful, because it diminishes the power to live. But bright sadness works differently. In Spinoza’s terms, the affects in it are mixed: sadness over what has passed or is out of reach, and joy in the memory itself, in beauty, in love for what was lost. It is precisely this joy that makes the sadness “bright.” Spinoza advised understanding your affects, and understanding, in his view, brings joy of its own. So there’s no need to fear this state: stay in it for a while, make out the love in it — and notice that it doesn’t take from you, but in its own way nourishes you.
melancholy.practice: Ask yourself: what is this sadness about, and what in it is dear to me? Write down one word for the sorrow and one for the tenderness.
